lessons.title: Opening Workplace Hook: The Email Policy Trap
lessons.content: Understand why sending a sustainability policy by email is not enough to create role clarity, accessible learning, or reliable training evidence across a diverse workforce.

contentBlocks.headingText: Opening Workplace Hook: The Email Policy Trap

contentBlocks.bodyText:
A growing hospitality and logistics enterprise in Mauritius introduces a new workplace sustainability policy and sends it as a PDF email attachment to all employees.

Three months later, HR reports a 98% email delivery rate as proof that the workforce understands sustainability. However, an internal operational review reveals:
• New hires recruited last month never received the policy.
• Frontline kitchen, maintenance, and warehouse staff with limited computer access were omitted.
• Department managers give conflicting instructions on waste sorting and water leak reporting.
• Training records consist of an incomplete Excel spreadsheet.
• Employees report that they do not know which specific sustainability expectations apply to their daily roles.
Sending an email attachment is an administrative delivery action. It does not prove role clarity, accessible learning, manager alignment, or operational understanding.

contentBlocks.decisionPrompt: A recruitment specialist wants to include the sentence 'Our company is 100% carbon neutral and eco-friendly' on all job vacancy advertisements to attract young talent. The company has carbon reduction initiatives underway, but has not completed Scope 1–3 audits or third-party carbon neutrality certification. How should the HR lead respond?

decisionChoices.label: Refuse the unverified claim and describe verified initiatives accurately (e.g., 'committed to workplace sustainability with on-site solar energy and formal waste reduction programmes')
decisionChoices.feedback: Correct! Employer branding must be truthful and grounded in verified policy. Unsubstantiated claims in recruitment create greenwashing risk and erode candidate trust.

decisionChoices.label: Approve the claim because job advertisements are just marketing and do not require factual evidence
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Employer recruitment statements must be factually defensible and compliant with advertising standards.

decisionChoices.label: Delete all references to sustainability from company careers pages permanently
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Promoting genuine, verified sustainability practices is great for talent acquisition—the key is factual accuracy.

lessons.title: Why HR Matters: Employee, Business and Environmental Relevance
lessons.content: Examine how HR acts as an enabler, coordinator, and evidence custodian across three key organizational levels.

contentBlocks.headingText: Why HR Matters for Workplace Sustainability

contentBlocks.bodyText:
HR enables workplace sustainability by embedding clear expectations from day one, ensuring accessible learning, supporting managers, and maintaining reliable training evidence.

• Employee Relevance: Employees gain clear expectations from onboarding, receive accessible learning in protected working hours, and know how to report operational barriers without fear of penalty.
• Business Relevance: Reliable training records protect company credibility, streamline internal and external audits, and prevent cross-departmental confusion.
• Environmental Relevance: Workforce training directly supports operational controls (e.g., proper waste sorting, energy shutoff SOPs) rather than remaining an isolated academic exercise.

lessons.title: HR Role Boundaries: Enabler vs Technical Owner
lessons.content: Define strict functional boundaries between HR responsibilities and operational, facilities, ESG, legal, or health and safety ownership.

contentBlocks.bodyText:
HR is an enabler and custodian—not the final technical decision-maker or environmental engineer. HR must never unilaterally interpret environmental laws, calculate carbon emissions, approve green claims, or select technical waste contractors.

Responsibility Matrix:
• Onboarding & Learning: HR coordinates and logs; Manager/ESG lead approves content.
• Technical SOPs: Operations/Facilities owns; HR supports role documentation.
• Environmental Claims: Marketing/Technical lead verifies; HR ensures recruitment materials match evidence.
• Health & Safety Risks: HSE Lead owns; HR documents employee reports and escalates immediately.

contentBlocks.decisionIntro: Competency matrix and shift training dilemma:
contentBlocks.decisionPrompt: A hotel operations manager insists that night-shift stewarding staff do not have time for sustainability training during working hours, and suggests having them sign the attendance register without completing the module. How should HR handle this?

decisionChoices.label: Refuse sign-off without real training; work with the manager to schedule 15-minute micro-learning blocks during protected shift changeover times
decisionChoices.feedback: Spot on! Signing off training that never occurred is fraudulent record-keeping (ISO 14001 Clause 7.2 failure). HR must enable accessible learning within paid working hours.

decisionChoices.label: Allow the manager to sign off everyone to maintain a 100% training completion metric on paper
decisionChoices.feedback: Severe governance failure! Falsified training records destroy audit integrity and leave frontline workers untrained on critical waste/chemical safety.

decisionChoices.label: Tell the stewarding staff they must complete the training at home on their personal phones without pay
decisionChoices.feedback: Unacceptable. Mandatory job training must occur during paid working hours with appropriate access.

lessons.title: Sourced Fact: From Awareness to Technical Competence
lessons.content: Distinguish between general awareness, understanding, technical capability, and decision authority using international standard principles.

contentBlocks.headingText: Sourced Fact: Awareness vs Technical Competence

contentBlocks.bodyText:
According to ISO 14001:2015 Clause 7.2 (Competence) and Clause 7.3 (Awareness):
• Awareness means an employee recognizes the environmental policy, understands how their work affects outcomes, and knows the consequences of non-conformance.
• Competence requires demonstrated capability based on education, training, or experience to perform specific tasks affecting environmental performance.

HR must recognize that general awareness training is not a substitute for technical competence certification (e.g. hazardous chemical handling or refrigerant recovery).

lessons.title: Six Key HR Responsibilities Across the Employee Lifecycle
lessons.content: Explore the six practical areas where HR supports workplace sustainability.

contentBlocks.bodyText:
1. Onboarding Integration: Introduce practical workplace habits and reporting channels from Day 1.
2. Role Clarity: Clarify sustainability boundaries within job descriptions.
3. Accessible Learning: Provide training during paid working hours in relevant languages and formats.
4. Performance Support: Enable constructive feedback without coercive naming or punitive shaming.
5. Training Evidence: Maintain auditable completion records with timestamps, versions, and assessment scores.
6. Inclusive Participation: Foster voluntary green team engagement and recognition.

contentBlocks.decisionPrompt: To boost employee engagement, an enthusiastic committee chair proposes creating a public 'Wall of Shame' displaying names of staff who missed monthly recycling targets. What is HR's role?

decisionChoices.label: Intervene immediately and redirect the approach toward positive recognition, removing operational friction, and constructive manager coaching
decisionChoices.feedback: Outstanding! Public shaming damages psychological safety, creates resentment, and violates HR principles. Sustainable engagement relies on removing barriers and positive recognition.

decisionChoices.label: Support the Wall of Shame because peer pressure is the fastest way to change behavior
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Coercive shaming destroys team morale and leads to hidden waste rather than genuine compliance.

decisionChoices.label: Institute salary deductions for any employee whose name appears on the wall
decisionChoices.feedback: Illegal and unethical. Unauthorized punitive salary deductions violate labor standards.

lessons.title: Step-by-Step Implementation: The HR Roadmap
lessons.content: Walk through the four-step roadmap to integrate sustainability into HR workflows.

contentBlocks.bodyText:
• Step 1: Baseline Assessment: Audit existing onboarding modules, job descriptions, and training records.
• Step 2: Role-Based Learning Paths: Map relevant ELEVIO courses to job functions (Foundation for all, Role-Specific for specialists).
• Step 3: Manager Alignment: Equip line supervisors to reinforce habits and provide protected learning time.
• Step 4: Audit-Ready Governance: Maintain synchronized records connecting learner IDs, course versions, and completion timestamps.

quizQuestions.question: What is the primary boundary of HR's role in workplace sustainability?
options: HR is the sole decision-maker for all facility emissions calculations and hazardous waste permits.
HR is an enabler, coordinator, and evidence custodian across the employee lifecycle, but does not own technical environmental engineering or compliance decisions.
HR has no role in sustainability because sustainability only concerns facilities engineering.
HR's role is strictly limited to organizing annual corporate social responsibility tree-planting events.

quizQuestions.question: What is the most effective and ethical way for HR to support employee engagement in sustainability initiatives?
options: Force employees to complete training during unpaid personal leave.
Publicly post names of employees who miss recycling targets on a 'Wall of Shame'.
Deduct money from monthly salaries if departmental energy targets are not met.
Create accessible learning opportunities, foster psychological safety, recognize positive contributions, and remove operational friction.

quizQuestions.question: According to ISO 14001:2015 Clauses 7.2 and 7.3 principles, what is the relationship between general awareness and technical competence?
options: General awareness ensures employees understand policy and reporting, while technical competence requires specific training and demonstrated capability for tasks with significant environmental impact.
General awareness and technical competence are identical and interchangeable.
Awareness is required only for board directors, while competence applies only to interns.
Competence eliminates the need for any workplace awareness training.

quizQuestions.question: A company sends a PDF sustainability policy attachment by email to all employees and reports a 98% email delivery rate as proof of workforce competence. Why is this insufficient?
options: Delivery rates must always exceed 99.9% before a policy can be considered valid.
Email attachments are legally prohibited in corporate communication under Mauritian labor law.
Email delivery proves transmission, but does not verify accessible learning, operational comprehension, frontline access, or role clarity.
Policies must always be hand-written on recycled parchment paper to be valid.

quizQuestions.question: What constitutes an audit-ready training evidence record maintained by HR?
options: Verifiable digital records tracking learner identification, course version, completion timestamps, and assessment scores.
An unsigned, undated bullet list of departmental staff names.
A verbal confirmation from a manager during a lunch break.
A photo of employees sitting in an auditorium without an attendance register.

quizQuestions.question: When drafting job descriptions and recruitment advertisements, what standard must HR uphold regarding sustainability?
options: Use unverified terms like '100% Eco-Friendly' and 'Zero Carbon' on all job posts to attract candidates.
Ensure environmental claims are factual, verified by policy evidence, and clearly describe actual role-based responsibilities.
Never mention sustainability because candidates are uninterested in corporate values.
Copy another company's recruitment brochure word-for-word.

quizQuestions.question: Why must employee sustainability training be conducted during paid working hours rather than personal time?
options: It allows the company to deduct training hours from statutory annual leave.
It is legally mandatory only for executive directors earning over a certain salary threshold.
Employees are not allowed to think about sustainability outside of office buildings.
It treats sustainability as a legitimate core operational job expectation, complies with fair labor standards, and ensures equal access for all shift workers.

quizQuestions.question: How should HR collaborate with line managers when an employee identifies an operational barrier to sustainability (e.g. broken sorting bins or missing PPE)?
options: Ignore the report because physical equipment issues are outside HR's jurisdiction.
Discipline the reporting employee for causing unnecessary administrative work.
Facilitate constructive communication between the employee, manager, and facilities to resolve the barrier without blaming the reporting employee.
Instruct the employee to purchase replacement equipment with their personal money.

ELH-26.title: Sustainability for Procurement and Purchasing Teams

lessons.title: Opening Hook: The Urgent Request
lessons.content: A realistic Mauritius procurement situation where an urgent order arrives with incomplete evidence and an undisclosed relationship.

contentBlocks.bodyText:
A department head at a Port Louis commercial property management company forwards an urgent message: 'We need to order twenty premium air-purification units immediately — the supplier discount expires Friday. I have already chosen the brand. Please process the order.'

Attached to the message is a single supplier quote describing the units as '100% eco-certified and carbon neutral'.

The procurement officer has thirty minutes before a weekly approval meeting.

The verified operational need — how many units are actually required and why?
A comparison of more than one supplier or option.
Evidence supporting the 'eco-certified and carbon neutral' claim.
Whether the department head has a personal or commercial relationship with the supplier.
A whole-life cost estimate including maintenance and replacement.
Required approval for a purchase of this value.
contentBlocks.headingText: What Is Missing from This Request?

contentBlocks.bodyText: This course prepares you to respond to situations like this — not by blocking necessary purchases, but by asking the right questions, collecting the right evidence, and recording a decision that can be defended on review.

lessons.title: Why Procurement Decisions Matter
lessons.content: Why sustainable procurement practices matter for employees, organisations and the environment.

contentBlocks.bodyText:
For you personally: Procurement decisions that are poorly documented or based on unverified claims create professional risk. A clear, evidence-based process protects the employee as much as the organisation.

For the business: Purchases are one of the most direct ways an organisation creates waste, incurs cost and generates environmental impact. Procurement decisions that consider whole-life value and supplier reliability reduce both financial and reputational risk.

For the environment and ESG: Supply chains account for a significant share of most organisations' environmental footprint. Procurement that asks the right questions about materials, energy use, packaging and end-of-life disposal can reduce that footprint without requiring specialist technical knowledge.

Purchasing without verifying the need leads to excess stock and waste.
Accepting unverified environmental claims creates greenwashing risk.
Ignoring whole-life costs results in higher total expenditure.
Failing to document decisions makes reviews and audits unreliable.
Undisclosed conflicts of interest undermine fair supplier selection.

lessons.title: Key Terms in Procurement and Purchasing
lessons.content: Plain-language definitions of the terms procurement employees genuinely need for sustainability-related purchasing decisions.

contentBlocks.headingText: Key Terms in Procurement and Purchasing

contentBlocks.bodyText:
Specification: A written description of what is being purchased — the function, performance standard, quantity and any relevant criteria. A vague specification produces vague supplier responses.

Whole-Life Cost (Total Cost of Ownership): The full cost of a purchase over its useful life, including price, installation, maintenance, consumables, energy or water use, and end-of-life disposal or return.

Evaluation Criteria: The specific factors against which supplier responses are compared. Criteria must be defined before responses are received and applied consistently throughout.

Greenwashing: Describing a product, service or organisation as environmentally responsible using claims that are vague, exaggerated, selective or unsupported by verifiable evidence.

Conflict of Interest: A personal, financial or professional relationship that could — or could appear to — influence a procurement decision unfairly. Must be declared and handled through the organisation's process.

Post-Award Management: The process of monitoring and managing a supplier after a contract or purchase order has been placed, to verify that agreed requirements are being met.

Take-Back Arrangement: A commitment by a supplier to collect or accept the return of a product or packaging at end of use, to prevent it going to landfill.

lessons.title: Procurement Role and Responsibility Boundaries
lessons.content: What procurement owns, coordinates, supports, escalates and does not independently authorise.

contentBlocks.bodyText:
Procurement owns: Verifying the operational need. Writing clear, proportionate specifications. Conducting a consistent supplier evaluation. Recording the reasoning behind a decision. Managing suppliers against agreed requirements. Raising concerns about claims, conflicts or process irregularities.

Procurement coordinates: The approval process for purchases above delegation thresholds. Technical or specialist verification of environmental, safety or legal claims. Finance review for capital expenditure and whole-life cost modelling.

Procurement supports: ESG and sustainability reporting by providing accurate decision records. Finance by supplying purchase documentation and supplier performance data. Operations and facilities by confirming that agreed requirements are in writing.

Procurement escalates: Conflict-of-interest concerns — to the organisation's designated process. Unverifiable or potentially misleading supplier claims — to a technical or sustainability lead. Process irregularities (such as criteria changed after offers are received) — to management or compliance.

Procurement does not independently: Make technical environmental assessments. Interpret legal or regulatory requirements. Guarantee supplier financial stability or capacity. Certify a product or service as compliant with a standard it has not assessed.

Completion of this course demonstrates familiarity with practical procurement principles. It is not a professional procurement licence, legal authorisation or technical qualification. It does not certify the learner to make independent environmental assessments or legal determinations.

lessons.title: Start With the Need, Not the Product
lessons.content: Before requesting a purchase, define what the organisation actually needs. Automatic replacement can create unnecessary cost and waste.

contentBlocks.headingText: Start With the Need, Not the Product

contentBlocks.bodyText: A purchasing request often names a specific product, brand or supplier before anyone has confirmed what the organisation actually needs. Starting with the product can lead to unnecessary spend, excess stock and wasted resources. Starting with the need gives procurement a clearer basis for any decision.

Is the item genuinely needed right now? Can an existing item be repaired, shared, reused or reassigned? What quantity is actually required? What performance or service outcome is needed? Is the request temporary, recurring or long-term?
contentBlocks.headingText: Questions to Ask Before Requesting a Purchase

contentBlocks.bodyText: Procurement should not pressure staff to avoid purchases that are necessary. Safety, quality, hygiene, accessibility and operational continuity remain essential. The goal is to ensure that what is purchased reflects a verified need, in the right quantity, for the right reason.

A hotel department requests twenty new office chairs because several chairs look worn. The procurement officer checks which chairs are structurally damaged, which can be repaired or reupholstered locally, whether unused chairs exist in another department, and whether all twenty are needed immediately. The decision may still be to purchase chairs — but the quantity and specification should be based on the verified need.

contentBlocks.decisionIntro: A department requests twelve new desktop printers, citing that their current printers are slow.
contentBlocks.decisionPrompt: Which is the strongest first action?

decisionChoices.label: Order the requested model immediately to avoid further delay.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Acting before confirming the need may result in unnecessary purchase of equipment that duplicates existing capacity.

decisionChoices.label: Ask what printing demand cannot be met by the existing shared printers.
decisionChoices.feedback: Correct. Clarifying the unmet operational need gives procurement the right basis for any decision — including whether new printers are actually required.

decisionChoices.label: Reject the request because printing creates waste.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Printing may be operationally necessary. A blanket rejection without reviewing the need is not proportionate.

decisionChoices.label: Choose the cheapest printer available online without further review.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Selecting by lowest price alone, without confirming the need or reviewing whole-life costs, can increase long-term operational expenditure.

lessons.title: Write Clear Requirements and Evaluate Evidence
lessons.content: Translate a sustainability intention into usable purchasing requirements and learn how verifiable evidence differs from marketing language.

contentBlocks.bodyText: Requirements must be relevant to the product or service being purchased. Vague instructions such as 'must be eco-friendly', 'must be green' or 'must be sustainable' are difficult to evaluate and can disqualify capable suppliers unfairly. Better criteria describe an observable feature, service or evidence.

Durability and expected lifespan. Repairability and local maintenance support. Energy or water performance. Packaging format and refill options. Use of recycled or responsibly sourced materials. Availability of replacement parts. Take-back or return arrangements. Delivery frequency. Supplier reporting or evidence commitments.

Criteria must remain proportionate. They should not unnecessarily prevent capable suppliers from competing. Do not invent mandatory certifications or legal requirements. Where specialist or legal advice is needed, escalate appropriately rather than making assumptions.

ISO 20400:2017 (Sustainable Procurement guidance) identifies specificity as the most important characteristic of a usable sustainability requirement. A requirement that describes a measurable outcome — such as 'minimum five-year manufacturer warranty with local service available within 48 hours' — allows all suppliers to respond on equal terms and allows evaluators to compare responses consistently. General statements such as 'must be environmentally responsible' cannot be evaluated or compared and carry a risk of legal challenge in competitive procurement.
contentBlocks.factTitle: Worth Knowing: Specific Criteria Produce Specific Responses

contentBlocks.bodyText: Instead of requesting 'environmentally friendly cleaning products', a workplace may ask shortlisted suppliers to provide: product-use instructions, packaging format and refill options, safety documentation required by company procedure, information supporting specific environmental claims, and delivery and container-return arrangements where available. Each criterion is specific and reviewable.

lessons.title: Compare Whole-Life Value, Not Price Alone
lessons.content: The cheapest initial price is not automatically the best value. Whole-life value accounts for the cost and operational consequences of a purchase over its useful life.

contentBlocks.headingText: Compare Whole-Life Value, Not Price Alone

contentBlocks.bodyText: Whole-life value means considering what a purchase will cost — and how it will perform — across its full useful life, not only at the point of purchase. A product with a lower purchase price may cost more to run, maintain or replace than one that costs more to buy initially.

Purchase price. Delivery and installation. Energy or water consumption during use. Consumables and replacement parts. Maintenance and repair costs. Expected useful life. Downtime or service disruption risk. Disposal or recovery arrangements at end of life. Contract management effort and supplier support.

The highest-priced option is not automatically the most sustainable choice either. The level of analysis should match the value, risk and duration of the purchase. Not every purchase requires a complex calculation — but recording the key assumptions and comparisons used helps justify the decision.

Two water dispensers are compared for an office. Option A has a lower purchase price but expensive proprietary filters and limited local servicing. Option B costs more initially but has locally available maintenance, standard replacement parts and a longer warranty. The decision should document the expected use, support arrangements and cost implications, rather than relying only on the purchase price.

contentBlocks.decisionIntro: A procurement officer is comparing two cleaning-equipment suppliers. Supplier A offers a lower purchase price. Supplier B offers a higher purchase price but includes a three-year maintenance contract with local technicians.
contentBlocks.decisionPrompt: What information is most useful before making a decision?

decisionChoices.label: The lowest purchase price, because procurement must always reduce upfront costs.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Upfront cost is one factor. Without reviewing maintenance costs and equipment lifespan, a lower purchase price may result in higher overall expenditure.

decisionChoices.label: The expected useful life, annual maintenance cost and local availability of spare parts for both options.
decisionChoices.feedback: Correct. These factors allow a more complete comparison of whole-life value, which is more useful than purchase price alone.

decisionChoices.label: Which supplier has a better sustainability brand reputation.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Brand reputation is not a substitute for specific, documented cost and performance information.

decisionChoices.label: Which supplier is larger, because larger organisations are more reliable.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Organisation size does not determine suitability. The evaluation should use the criteria stated in the specification.

lessons.title: The Procurement Cycle: A Visual Guide
lessons.content: A visual guide to the six-stage sustainable procurement cycle, with an interactive interpretation question.

contentBlocks.captionText: The six-stage procurement cycle: Define Need → Write Requirements → Compare Value & Evidence → Approve & Document → Confirm Agreement → Review Supplier Performance.

contentBlocks.bodyText:
Reading the diagram: Each stage has a defined output before the next stage can proceed.

Stage 1 — Define Need: Output is a confirmed requirement with verified quantity.
Stage 2 — Write Requirements: Output is a specification with observable criteria.
Stage 3 — Compare Value and Evidence: Output is a consistent evaluation against stated criteria.
Stage 4 — Approve and Document: Output is a defensible decision note with required approvals.
Stage 5 — Confirm Agreement: Output is a written purchase order or contract confirming requirements.
Stage 6 — Review Supplier Performance: Output is a performance record against agreed requirements.

If Stage 6 is skipped, the organisation has no documented basis for renewing, improving or challenging the supplier arrangement.

lessons.title: Test Supplier Claims and Evidence
lessons.content: Environmental claims from suppliers require appropriate scrutiny. Ask the right questions rather than accepting or dismissing claims without review.

contentBlocks.bodyText: Suppliers sometimes describe their products or services using terms such as 'zero impact', '100% green', 'carbon neutral', 'fully biodegradable' or 'planet friendly'. These phrases may be accurate, partially accurate, or difficult to verify. Procurement employees do not need to assess the technical accuracy of every claim — but they should ask useful questions before accepting or repeating one.

What exactly does this claim apply to? Which product, period or service is covered? What conditions or limitations apply? What evidence supports it? Is that evidence current and relevant to the product or service offered? Does the claim apply to the full product, or only a component?

Supplier brochures alone may not answer every question. Evidence requirements should remain proportionate to the value and risk of the purchase. Unsupported claims should not receive evaluation credit merely because they sound positive. Concerns should be recorded and escalated through the organisation's approval process.

A packaging supplier describes a product as 'fully biodegradable in Mauritius'. The buyer asks: Under which conditions does it break down? Does it require industrial treatment? What evidence supports the claim? Does the claim apply to the full packaging item, including labels and lining? The buyer records the supplier's response rather than repeating the original claim as fact in the evaluation report.

contentBlocks.decisionIntro: Three suppliers each make a statement about their product. You need to identify the most decision-useful statement.
contentBlocks.decisionPrompt: Which statement is most useful when comparing supplier evidence?

decisionChoices.label: Our product protects the planet.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. This is a general marketing statement with no specific claim, evidence or measurement. It cannot be evaluated or compared.

decisionChoices.label: Our packaging contains recycled material.
decisionChoices.feedback: Partially useful but incomplete. The proportion, type of recycled material and supporting evidence are not specified. This statement cannot be reliably compared between suppliers.

decisionChoices.label: The offered container contains 40% post-consumer recycled plastic by weight, supported by the attached product specification from our manufacturer.
decisionChoices.feedback: Correct. This statement is specific, measurable and supported by documentation. It allows for a fair comparison between suppliers and can be recorded in the evaluation.

decisionChoices.label: We are committed to sustainability and reducing our environmental impact across all operations.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. A general commitment statement does not provide specific, verifiable information about the product being purchased.

lessons.title: Scenario Challenge: The Cleaning Contract Renewal
lessons.content: A multi-step Mauritius workplace scenario requiring the learner to review evidence, respect role boundaries and choose a practical response.

contentBlocks.headingText: Scenario Challenge: The Cleaning Contract Renewal

contentBlocks.bodyText:
A hotel in Grand Baie, Mauritius, is renewing its three-year cleaning-services contract. Three suppliers have responded. The procurement officer has received the following:

Supplier A: Lowest price. States products are '100% natural and certified zero-impact'. No supporting documentation provided.

Supplier B: Mid-range price. Provides product data sheets, a refill and take-back arrangement, and a written maintenance schedule. Prices include all consumables.

Supplier C: Highest price. The operations manager has mentioned privately that they have used the supplier personally for home services and finds them reliable.

The operations manager is pressing for a quick decision before the current contract expires on Friday.

Step 1: Note that Supplier A's claim ('100% natural and certified zero-impact') is unspecified. Ask what evidence supports it before awarding evaluation points. Record the response.

Step 2: Note that the operations manager has a personal connection to Supplier C. This must be declared and handled through the conflict-of-interest process before evaluation proceeds — regardless of the manager's intention or the quality of Supplier C's service.

Step 3: Evaluate all three suppliers against the agreed criteria (quality, whole-life cost, documented sustainability commitments, local service availability). Based on available evidence, Supplier B provides the most specific and verifiable information.

Step 4: Record the evaluation, including how Supplier A's claim was handled, how the declared connection to Supplier C was managed, and why Supplier B met the stated criteria. Do not accuse the manager of misconduct.

Step 5: Confirm the agreement with the selected supplier in writing, including specific requirements, and assign responsibility for monitoring performance.
contentBlocks.headingText: What Does the Procurement Officer Do?

contentBlocks.decisionIntro: The operations manager insists that Supplier C should be selected because 'they are the best in the business'. The conflict-of-interest declaration has not yet been made.
contentBlocks.decisionPrompt: What is the correct procurement response?

decisionChoices.label: Select Supplier C immediately, because management preferences take priority.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Proceeding without a declared conflict-of-interest is a process failure that exposes the organisation and the procurement officer to review risk, regardless of whether Supplier C is actually the strongest option.

decisionChoices.label: Require the personal connection to be declared through the conflict-of-interest process before proceeding, and apply the evaluation criteria consistently to all three suppliers.
decisionChoices.feedback: Correct. A declared connection, handled through the established process, allows the evaluation to proceed fairly. This protects the organisation, the manager and the procurement officer.

decisionChoices.label: Remove Supplier C from consideration immediately to avoid any appearance of bias.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Excluding a supplier without due process may itself be unfair and creates a different risk. The connection must be declared and the process followed — then the evaluation result determines the outcome.

decisionChoices.label: Ask the manager to confirm in writing that the connection will not affect their judgement.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. A written assurance alone does not satisfy conflict-of-interest requirements. The formal declaration and process must be followed.

lessons.title: Make and Record a Defensible Decision
lessons.content: A procurement decision is defensible when the reasoning, information reviewed and approvals followed are clearly recorded.

contentBlocks.headingText: Make and Record a Defensible Decision

contentBlocks.bodyText: Applying evaluation criteria consistently and recording the process is a professional responsibility, not an administrative burden. Records support internal review, budget control, supplier management, ESG evidence and consistency in future purchases.

The verified need. Shortlisted options considered. Information reviewed and key assumptions. Any missing evidence and how it was handled. The evaluation result against stated criteria. Required approvals and who provided them. The final reason for selection.

Avoid vague decision notes such as 'best supplier', 'most sustainable' or 'preferred option'. These phrases do not explain the reasoning and cannot be reviewed meaningfully. Do not change evaluation criteria informally after offers have been received — criteria must be applied consistently throughout the process.

Personal relationships, gifts or undisclosed interests must not influence supplier selection. If a conflict exists or may appear to exist, it must be declared and handled through the organisation's approval and escalation process. The procurement officer should not attempt to resolve a conflict of interest alone.

A manager prefers a supplier they have used privately. The procurement officer does not accuse the manager of misconduct. Instead, they ensure the relationship is declared and that the organisation's evaluation and approval process is followed. The decision record documents that the declared relationship was noted and that the process remained consistent.

contentBlocks.decisionIntro: A procurement officer has selected a supplier for cleaning equipment. They need to write a decision note.
contentBlocks.decisionPrompt: Which decision note is strongest?

decisionChoices.label: Supplier B was selected because they are the most sustainable option on the market.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. This is an unsupported claim. 'Most sustainable' does not explain the specific evaluation criteria used or how Supplier B performed against them.

decisionChoices.label: Supplier B was selected as the best overall value based on price, service record and delivery reliability.
decisionChoices.feedback: Partially useful, but it does not specify the evaluation criteria stated in the original requirement or how each supplier performed against those criteria.

decisionChoices.label: Supplier B was selected because it met all three evaluation criteria: ten-year expected lifespan per product specification, local maintenance support within 48 hours, and a documented take-back arrangement. Supplier A did not provide evidence of local maintenance support.
decisionChoices.feedback: Correct. This note states the criteria applied, how each supplier performed, and the specific reason for selection. It is clear, consistent and reviewable.

decisionChoices.label: Supplier B was selected because we have worked with them before and they are reliable.
decisionChoices.feedback: Incorrect. Prior relationship is not a stated evaluation criterion and may raise conflict-of-interest concerns without a clear record of the evaluation process.

lessons.title: Manage the Supplier After Award
lessons.content: Sustainability-related procurement does not end when a purchase order or contract is issued. Performance must be monitored and problems addressed early.

contentBlocks.bodyText: A purchase order or contract confirms what has been agreed. Confirming requirements in writing, assigning responsibility for checking performance, and reviewing delivery against what was agreed are part of completing the procurement process — not an optional extra.

Product quality and quantities delivered. Packaging format versus what was agreed. Maintenance visits and service frequency. Waste removal or take-back arrangements. Reporting commitments. Agreed corrective actions.

Procurement staff should distinguish between a one-off issue, repeated poor performance, and a requirement that was never clearly documented. Discussing problems early and specifically — with a record of the discussion — avoids disputes and helps both parties improve. Renewal points are useful opportunities to improve the specification for the next contract period.

A supplier agreed to collect reusable delivery crates but repeatedly leaves them onsite. The contract owner records the missed collections, contacts the supplier, agrees a corrective action with a deadline, and notes in the file whether the original requirement was clearly stated. At renewal, the requirement is written more specifically into the next agreement.

Practical Actions to Apply Now:
• Clarify the operational need before naming a product in a purchase request.
• Replace vague 'eco-friendly' wording with a specific, verifiable criterion.
• Ask for evidence when a supplier makes a material environmental claim — and record the response.
• Write decision notes that state the criteria, the evaluation result and the reason for selection.
• Review one recurring contract for a requirement that is agreed but not being verified.
• Declare personal connections early and follow the conflict-of-interest process.

commitmentOptions.label: I will clarify the operational need before naming a product.
commitmentOptions.description: Confirming what is genuinely needed prevents unnecessary purchases.

commitmentOptions.description: Clear requirements produce useful supplier responses.

commitmentOptions.description: Specific evidence supports a fair evaluation.

commitmentOptions.label: I will record the reasons for a supplier decision against stated criteria.
commitmentOptions.description: Clear records support review, consistency and ESG evidence.
